To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

LAS is found in sewage sludge in high concentration, that the limit proposed by EU for LAS would make difficult the disposal of most sewage sludge in Spain, and that the anaerobic degradation of soap is not a relevant mechanism for the occurrence of soap in sludge, but the anaerobic fate of LAS is.

LAS is the most abundant synthetic anionic surfactive in Spanish sewage sludges, and that the implementation of its limit in the European sewage sludge Directive would make the disposal for agricultural application almost impossible.
the average concentration of LAS in Spanish sludge is higher and the average biodegradability in anaerobic conditions is lower than in the EU.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the need to revise the proposed cut-off limit for anionic surfactans in sludge and the need to consider other parameters, such as the biodegradation potential of the surfactants, in the decision-making process.
the monitoring of organic chemicals in sewage sludge and the evaluation of their environmental impact, in order to help in the revision of the sewage sludge European Directive.
the environmental impact of anionic surfactans in sewage sludge, which may have an important role in the implementation of the new European sewage sludge Directive.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LAS is not an environmental hazard for agricultural applications, as it is not for any other environmental compartment.
the use of sewage sludge for agricultural purposes would be limited in most European countries if the proposed limits were implemented, due to the presence of LAS and soap.
the implementation of a cut-off limit for LAS in the revised Sewage Sludge directive would be inappropriate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in spite of the fact that the anaerobic degradation of LAS and soap is well documented, the environmental risk associated to the application of sewage sludge to soil is not well understood, since the mechanisms of the anaerobically formed products are not known.
the disposal of most sludge in agriculture would be restricted due to the presence of high amounts of surfactants.

the use of LAS in the detergent industry should be reduced to avoid the presence of high amounts of this surfactant in sewage sludge, which would be the only way to avoid the impossibility of using sludge in agriculture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cut-off value for LAS proposed by the 4th European Working paper on sewage sludge is not appropriate for Spanish sludge.
, if a cut-off limit is implemented for anionic surfactans, it should not be based on the biodegradation in aerobic conditions, but rather on the biodegradability in anaerobic conditions.
the implementation of a limit for LAS in sludge will not be effective to protect the environment.
